title: Design exercise: ride matching and location
summary: A classic design exercise: matching riders to nearby drivers from a location stream, with one driver per trip and one active offer per ride. The answer filters positions by session sequence and event freshness, ranks candidates behind an ETA deadline, and atomically coordinates ride and driver state with conditional fencing tokens.

exercise.prompt: Design the matching system of a ride-hailing product: drivers stream their location, a rider requests a trip, and the system finds a nearby driver, offers them the trip, and confirms the match. A driver must never be given two trips at once, and a rider must get an answer within seconds even when the map or traffic service is having a bad day.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Ingest driver locations; find candidate drivers near a pickup point; rank by estimated arrival time; offer the trip to one driver at a time with a timeout; confirm the match atomically so one driver has at most one active trip; expose supply and demand per area to a pricing service; keep location history for analysis.
100 cities; 1 million drivers online at peak sending a location every 4 s.
chosen for the exercise; derive the location update rate, the index memory and the match rate yourself
5 million ride requests per day, peak 10x the average; a candidate search radius that yields about 50 drivers in a dense area.
A match offered within 3 s at p95 and confirmed within 20 s at p95 (one offer round of 15 s); location freshness under 10 s.

99.95 percent availability for matching; the one-driver-one-trip invariant holds under every failure; degraded matching (coarser ranking) is acceptable when the ETA service is down, no matching is not.
Pricing and surge computation itself, payments, routing and navigation inside the trip, fraud, pooled rides.

clarifying_questions.a: A fixed set of grid cells around the pickup; the grid is a hierarchical hexagonal index (H3: sixteen resolutions, each finer one seventh the area of the coarser), and the search expands ring by ring until enough candidates are found or a radius limit is hit.

clarifying_questions.q: Who is the single source of truth for a driver's state?
clarifying_questions.a: The driver lock store: a driver is free, offered or on a trip, and only the holder of the current lease may change it.

clarifying_questions.q: What if the driver does not answer the offer?
clarifying_questions.a: The offer times out after 15 s (assumption), the lock is released, and the next-ranked driver is offered. After three rounds the rider is told no driver was found.
By a routing service (a contraction-hierarchy routing engine over map data, as Uber describes) with a 100 ms deadline (assumption); straight-line distance is the fallback.
Yes: cities are the partition unit for the index and the matching service; a trip never crosses the partition at request time.

clarifying_questions.q: How long is location history kept?
clarifying_questions.a: 30 days raw in cold storage, aggregates longer (assumption).

blocks.text: Every number below follows from the stated assumptions: 1 million drivers online at peak sending a location every 4 s, 5 million ride requests a day with a peak at ten times the average, and about 50 candidates per search in a dense area. The tables carry the arithmetic; the paragraphs carry the assumptions.

one per match, for about 50 candidates each: about 30,000 candidate ETAs per second
retry rounds reuse ranked candidates with freshness checks; no extra ETA call in this model
a lease, an accept or a release per round; small beside the location rate

blocks.caption: Sizes: the live index and the history.
rows: the last position plus the cell membership (assumption)
1 million entries times 100 bytes payload; runtime structures, replicas and headroom are additional
continuous peak: 250,000 updates/s times 50 bytes; raw retention is 30 days. Average WebSocket occupancy is a separate assumption.
the rings around the pickup cell, up to 5 rings (assumption)

blocks.text: The historical 500-microsecond datacenter RTT is not a measurement of this AWS path. ETA deadlines, callback delivery and offer acceptance must be measured together. The human decision dominates the intended confirmation target, but a fast offer is an SLO assumption, not a guarantee from a latency gist.

Driver positions enter a city log as packed records. The gateway acknowledges only per-record durable successes; consumers compare authenticated session/sequence and event time rather than relying on arrival order. A per-city index keeps current grid membership, while the same stream feeds cold history and asynchronous supply/demand snapshots. The matcher finds nearby candidates, ranks with a bounded ETA call, and atomically acquires the ride and driver before sending an offer. The Ride API authenticates acceptance and changes both records in one transaction; no crash gap exists between on_trip and matched.

blocks.text: The grid is a hierarchical hexagonal index in the H3 shape: sixteen resolutions, each finer one with cells of one seventh the area of the coarser, so a search can expand ring by ring around the pickup cell; S2 is the alternative with the same hierarchical property on a sphere. ETAs come from a routing engine over map data; Uber's own engine is built on contraction hierarchies, which answer a route in milliseconds after preprocessing the graph.

blocks.text: The write path through AWS, part a: a batch of positions from the gateway to the city's index. Edge is the load balancer, drawn as one lane as in the other exercises; there is no CloudFront because nothing here is cacheable.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant D as Driver app
  participant Edge
  participant LG as Location gateway
  participant K as City stream
  participant GI as Geo index
  D->>Edge: authenticated position batch
  Edge->>LG: session and sequence
  LG->>K: PutRecords opaque aggregates
  K-->>LG: per-record results
  alt all records durable
    LG-->>Edge: 204
    Edge-->>D: 204
  else partial failure
    LG-->>Edge: retryable batch status
    Edge-->>D: retry or supersede old data
  end
  K-)GI: records may be reordered
  GI->>GI: newest sequence and freshness
blocks.legend: The gateway checks every PutRecords result before success. Failed records retry with the same sample identity; the client may explicitly supersede unacknowledged old positions, so this is not a lossless GPS archive. Index consumers reject older sessions/sequences and stale event times without refreshing TTL. City streams provide isolation, not source ordering. Sources: Kinesis s8/s9, endpoint s11, task replacement s25/s29 and PutRecords s45.

blocks.text: Both index tasks of a city read every shard of the city's stream, so each holds the whole city and either can serve a match; a replacement task replays only the last minutes, because older positions are stale by the freshness rule anyway. The gateway aggregates records per shard, since a shard accepts a thousand records a second and a batch of positions is many small records.
Part b: the same stream feeding the history and the supply-and-demand aggregates, which no match waits for.

blocks.text: The read path through AWS, part a: request identity and durable matching hand-off.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant R as Rider
  participant Edge
  participant API as Ride API
  participant DB as DynamoDB rides
  participant MS as Matcher
  R->>Edge: POST with client request id
  Edge->>API: authenticated intent
  API->>DB: conditional PutItem
  alt new key
    DB-->>API: stored ride
    API-)MS: wake hint, work already durable
    API-->>Edge: 202 ride identity
  else same key and payload
    DB-->>API: ALL_OLD with same hash
    API-->>Edge: 200 existing ride
  else same key different payload
    DB-->>API: ALL_OLD with other hash
    API-->>Edge: 409 conflict
  end
  Edge-->>R: response
  Note over DB,MS: recovery queries every bucket of the pending index
blocks.legend: The authenticated rider and preexisting client request id determine ride identity even after a lost response. Only a newly created key schedules the wake hint. A matching retry returns the existing ride, while a reused key with another canonical payload conflicts. The pending index is the durable hand-off, so a lost or failed hint cannot erase work. Sources: conditional writes s17, gateway endpoint s31, Service Connect s26 and task replacement s25.

blocks.text: Part c: the lease transaction and the offer pushed over the WebSocket.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 16
  participant MS as Matcher
  participant DB as Rides and driver state
  participant WS as WebSocket API
  participant D as Driver
  MS->>DB: transact fenced offer
  alt ride and driver claimed
    DB-->>MS: fence and deadline
    MS->>DB: GetItem current connection
    DB-->>MS: connection identity
    MS->>WS: signed callback via NAT
    WS-)D: offer and fence
  else conditional conflict

blocks.legend: A transaction claims both requested ride and free driver, increments the driver's persistent fence and stores the offer deadline. Concurrent matchers cannot claim two drivers for one ride. Only successful acquisition sends an offer. Lookup uses the authenticated driver's connection mapping; Gone conditionally deletes that mapping, timeout may duplicate the same offer. Reconnect reads the outstanding durable offer. Sources: transactions s47, WebSocket s22, callback endpoint limitation s46, fencing s6.

blocks.text: Part d: the accept with the fence, and the late accept that must be refused.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 23
  participant D as Driver
  participant Edge
  participant API as Ride API
  participant DB as Rides and driver state
  D->>Edge: accept ride and fence
  Edge->>API: authenticated driver
  API->>DB: transact accept conditions
  alt offered tuple and valid deadline
    DB-->>API: ride matched, driver on_trip
    API-->>Edge: 200 matched
  else condition failed or lost result
    API->>DB: consistent tuple read
    DB-->>API: current ride and driver
    API-->>Edge: same match 200, else 409
  end
  Edge-->>D: response
blocks.legend: The transaction checks offered state, authenticated driver, ride identity, fence and deadline, then writes matched/on_trip atomically. A lost success reply is recovered by reading the same matched tuple; a stale or expired offer is rejected even without a successor. Deadline is checked at trusted API admission using the explicit clock model below. Sources: transactional atomicity s47, conditional writes s16, gateway endpoint s31 and fencing s6.

blocks.text: Part e: a decline, and an offer nobody answered.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 32
  participant D as Driver
  participant Edge
  participant API as Ride API
  participant DB as Rides and driver state
  participant MS as Matcher
  alt explicit decline
    D->>Edge: decline ride and fence
    Edge->>API: authenticated driver
    API->>DB: transact release
    alt offered tuple still matches
      DB-->>API: ride requested, driver free
      API-)MS: wake pending ride
      API-->>Edge: 204 released
    else successor or active trip
      DB-->>API: condition failed, no change
      API-->>Edge: 409 current state
    end
    Edge-->>D: response
  else deadline passed unanswered
    Note over MS: reconciler queries every bucket of the pending index
    MS->>DB: transact release after the clock margin
    alt still offered
      DB-->>MS: ride requested, driver free
      MS->>MS: next ranked candidate
    else successor or active trip
      DB-->>MS: no change
    end
  end
blocks.legend: A decline travels the accept's route: the Ride API authenticates the driver, then one transaction releases both records only if the ride is still offered to this driver with this fence, writing the ride back to requested with its retry time set to now and the driver to free, and the fence is not touched. The API then sends the matcher a wake hint, which is only a nudge, because the pending index already holds the ride. A late or repeated decline fails the same conditions and changes nothing. An offer nobody answers is released by the reconciler, the matcher's recovery job, with the same transaction once the deadline has passed by the clock margin. Sources: transactions s47, conditional writes s16, gateway endpoint s31 and fencing s6.

blocks.text: The conditional transaction across ride and driver records decides the invariant, not a separate lock write followed by a ride write. Fail closed if that Regional database boundary is unavailable: a delayed match is preferable to double assignment.

blocks.caption: The driver lock store: DynamoDB, Aurora, MemoryDB, or ElastiCache.

rows.pick_when: ride and driver conditions fit a bounded same-Region transaction and key-shaped reads
rows.avoid_when: the access pattern requires ad hoc relational queries or cross-Region transactional guarantees
rows.example: For this design: chosen with TransactWriteItems across ride and driver state. Conditions enforce both one-driver-one-trip and one-offer-per-ride, rather than relying on an expiring field to change state automatically.

rows.pick_when: the team wants relational transactions over ride and driver state or SQL reporting
rows.avoid_when: key-shaped transactions fit the existing managed key-value platform better
rows.example: For this design: valid alternative. A database transaction absolutely buys atomicity here; this answer obtains it from DynamoDB transactions instead of separate writes.

rows.pick_when: measured workload and a verified durable concurrency protocol favor an in-memory database
rows.avoid_when: simple key transactions already satisfy the requirements
rows.example: For this design: not selected. A database category guide alone does not establish the lease, fencing or latency guarantees needed here; SET NX with expiry is not the full two-entity protocol.

rows.pick_when: the data is a cache that may be lost
rows.avoid_when: the data decides an invariant: a cache that loses the lock can grant the same driver twice
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for correctness-critical ownership. Kleppmann distinguishes efficiency locks from correctness locks; a rebuildable geo cache may tolerate loss, but assignment must preserve fenced state across failures.

blocks.caption: The location log: Kinesis provisioned per city, Kinesis on-demand, SQS FIFO, or Amazon MSK.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, provisioned shards, one stream per city
rows.pick_when: consumers need replay and known city-level isolation; application sequence checks handle producer retry/reordering
rows.avoid_when: the load swings by an order of magnitude within a day or the number of partitions is unknown
rows.example: For this design: chosen for city isolation and replay, not a claim that PutRecords orders updates. Consumers enforce authenticated session sequence and event freshness independently of arrival order.

rows.pick_when: the per-city rates are unknown or bursty and nobody wants to count shards
rows.avoid_when: steady bytes plus every independent reader and fixed per-stream charges exceed provisioned capacity cost
rows.example: For this design: price all city streams and all three readers, with physical-record rounding. The revised on-demand comparison is about $9,100, not the earlier two-reader estimate.

rows.pick_when: message-group ordering and queue-side deduplication fit one processing path, with idempotent application effects
rows.avoid_when: a consumer must replay from a position to rebuild state, or several consumers need the same records
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A replacement index task rebuilds by replaying the last minutes, and Firehose reads the same records; a queue has neither a position nor a second reader.

rows.pick_when: the team runs Kafka already, or needs topics, compression and retention beyond what the managed stream offers
rows.avoid_when: a hundred small partitions where brokers to size and patch buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen; a hundred streams of a few shards each need no brokers.

blocks.caption: The compute: ECS on Fargate, Lambda, EKS, or EC2.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services, including small stateful ones (the per-city index) whose state is rebuilt from a stream
rows.avoid_when: the state per task exceeds the task size, or the service needs the host (GPUs, local disk)
rows.example: For this design: chosen for everything: two index tasks and two matching tasks per city, the gateway, the ride API and the aggregator scaled on request rate, the ETA service sized on routes per second with the map in memory.

rows.pick_when: event-shaped work with spiky volume and no state between invocations
rows.avoid_when: a per-city index held in memory, or a matcher that must answer in a chain of sub-millisecond calls
rows.example: For this design: only for the WebSocket API's connect and disconnect routes, which record the driver's connection id; nothing on the match path.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and wants the per-city services as stateful sets with its operators
rows.avoid_when: a small platform team with no Kubernetes estate
rows.example: For this design: not chosen; the ECS scheduler, Service Connect and the stream replay give the per-city shape without a cluster to run.

rows.pick_when: the ETA service's map data outgrows a task's memory, or routing wants a particular instance family
rows.example: For this design: the alternative for the ETA service at 10x, when the routing engine's memory and CPU make a reserved instance family cheaper than large tasks.

blocks.caption: The geo index: in-task memory, ElastiCache for Valkey with GEOSEARCH, DynamoDB, or MemoryDB.

rows.option: In-task memory, two tasks per city, rebuilt from the stream
rows.pick_when: the live set is small, the query is a set lookup per cell, and the tasks can rebuild from a log in seconds
rows.avoid_when: many services need the same index, or the city's set outgrows a task
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the matcher and supply/demand snapshots. A hundred-megabyte global payload estimate does not prove per-city memory use; hundreds of megabytes per task is unbenchmarked overhead/headroom, not a derived payload.

rows.pick_when: several services query the same positions, or the team wants a radius query without writing the cell logic
rows.avoid_when: an update rate that would cost a cache node per city for what a task holds in memory
rows.example: For this design: the honest alternative. GEOSEARCH by radius from the pickup point replaces the ring logic, and a replica covers a node loss; it would be the pick if the ETA service or pricing also needed live positions.

rows.pick_when: positions must be durable and queryable by anyone
rows.avoid_when: 250,000 writes a second of data that is stale in 10 s
rows.example: For this design: not chosen; the write rate alone would cost about $400,000 a month in write units for positions nobody reads after a few seconds.

rows.pick_when: the positions are the system of record and must survive a node loss
rows.avoid_when: the positions are rebuildable from the stream in seconds
rows.example: For this design: not chosen; durability for data that expires in 10 s is paid for nothing.

The levers are consolidating quiet cities onto shared tasks and holding a connection only while a driver can receive an offer.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: One ride request in a dense area; the step numbers run on across the four parts.
Part a: the location path that keeps the index fresh, running continuously underneath every match.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant D as Driver
  participant LG as Location gateway
  participant LL as Location log
  participant GI as Geo index
  participant SD as Supply and demand
  D->>LG: authenticated positions
  LG->>LL: append packed records
  LL-->>LG: per-record durable results
  LG-->>D: ack successes, retry failures
  LL-)GI: duplicated or reordered data
  GI->>GI: session, sequence, event time
  GI-)SD: async cell snapshot
blocks.legend: Durable acknowledgement is per record. The application may drop superseded unacknowledged positions, not pretend they entered history. Older records never move a driver backwards or extend freshness. The same packed stream feeds history.

blocks.text: Part b: the request, the candidates from the rings, and the ranking with the ETA deadline.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 8
  participant R as Rider
  participant API as Ride API
  participant MS as Matcher
  participant GI as Geo index
  participant ETA
  R->>API: request with stable identity
  API->>API: persist requested work
  API-)MS: wake pending ride
  API-->>R: ride identity and state

  GI-->>MS: candidate set
  MS->>ETA: batched ETAs with deadline
  ETA-->>MS: times or fallback trigger

blocks.legend: The rings are H3 cells around the pickup cell s1; the ETA service is a routing engine of the contraction-hierarchy kind s4; the fairness term (time since the driver's last trip) is an assumption.

blocks.text: Part c: the lease, the offer, and the accept with the fencing token, which is where the one-driver-one-trip invariant is decided.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 16
  participant MS as Matcher
  participant DB as Ride and driver store
  participant D as Driver
  participant API as Ride API
  MS->>DB: atomic offer acquisition
  alt both states claimed
    DB-->>MS: fence and deadline
    MS-)D: offer with fence
    D->>API: authenticated accept
    API->>DB: atomic fenced acceptance
    alt valid offered tuple
      DB-->>API: matched and on_trip
      API-->>D: matched
    else expired or changed
      DB-->>API: reject or existing match
      API-->>D: response
    end
  else acquisition conflict
    DB-->>MS: no offer sent
  end
blocks.legend: The transactional store enforces ride exclusion and driver exclusion together. Fence values increase on each acquisition and never reset. Acceptance checks identity, offered state and admission deadline, not just token equality. This design implements conditional transactional ownership, informed by s5/s6 rather than claiming TTL alone provides safety.

blocks.text: Part d: timeout or decline, and the next candidate.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 26
  participant MS as Matcher
  participant DB as Ride and driver store
  participant D as Driver
  participant API as Ride API
  participant R as Rider
  alt explicit decline
    D->>API: decline ride and fence
    API->>DB: release matching offered tuple
    alt both conditions hold
      DB-->>API: free driver, requested ride
      API-)MS: wake pending ride
      MS->>MS: recheck next ranked candidate
    else successor or active trip
      DB-->>API: no change
    end
  else expired admission deadline
    Note over MS: recovery finds overdue offer
    MS->>DB: release matching offered tuple
    alt both conditions hold
      DB-->>MS: free driver, requested ride
      MS->>MS: recheck next ranked candidate
    else successor or active trip
      DB-->>MS: no change
    end
  end
  opt rounds exhausted
    MS->>DB: conditionally cancel requested ride
    alt cancelled
      DB-->>MS: cancelled
      MS-->>R: no driver found
    else matched or active
      DB-->>MS: current state
      MS-->>R: current ride state
    end
  end
blocks.legend: A deadline does not change stored state by itself, and a decline is released by the Ride API, as the accept is decided there. Release checks both records' state, ride and fence and never resets the driver fence. Retried cleanup is harmless because a successor or active trip fails those conditions. Retry rounds reuse the ranked candidates after freshness checks; they do not rerun ETA.

blocks.text: Per-city partitioning keeps every hot structure small: the index for the largest city is a few hundred thousand drivers, one process with a replica, consuming its share of the location log. The update rate is absorbed by the log and by batching in the app (several positions per request). The matching service is also per city and is where contention lives: two requests in the same block at the same second want the same best driver, and the compare-and-set on the lock store resolves it without a global lock.

DynamoDB is not a native timed lease service. Acquisition strongly reads the driver fence, then transacts driver free/version-equals-read and ride requested/version-equals-read conditions, storing the incremented fence and offer deadline on both records. A competing transaction changes those versions and forces a retry. Neither record is TTL-deleted; driver fences never reset. Accept requires both records offered with the same authenticated driver, ride, fence and admitted deadline; it atomically writes matched/on_trip. Lost replies use TransactGetItems to recover an already-matched tuple.

Time model: only authenticated service clocks decide admission, with monitored UTC error bounded by 250 ms. Accept requires stored_deadline greater than server_now plus that margin; expiry cleanup waits until server_now minus the margin passes the deadline. If clock health fails, fail closed. This is an admission deadline, not a promise of database commit before that instant; concurrent cleanup and acceptance still serialize on the same conditional transaction.

An authenticated connect CAS-increments a persistent driver-session epoch and stores the current connection mapping; the epoch is never deleted or reset. Disconnect/Gone conditionally remove only their own current connection fields, never a newer mapping. Matchers look up this mapping and sign public callbacks. Timeout may duplicate the same fenced offer; reconnect fetches that driver's outstanding offer through the authorized Ride API. API Gateway connections last at most two hours and idle out after ten minutes, so jittered reconnect is normal. Callback NAT assumes a conservative request/response byte allowance, not free PrivateLink.

Release requires both records still offered with the same ride/fence and either an authenticated decline or an expired admission deadline under the clock rule. It atomically returns the ride to requested and driver to free without changing the fence. A decline reaches the Ride API like an accept: the API authenticates the driver, runs this release as one transaction and sends the matcher a wake hint; an expired deadline is released the same way by the reconciler. A requested/offering sparse index persists until matched/cancelled and is partitioned by the city plus a ride-id bucket, which spreads a busy city's index writes over several partitions; the reconciler queries every bucket for overdue items, including matcher death after acquisition but before delivery, and conditionally releases or re-wakes it. Duplicate index results are safe. Cancel checks requested state/version, so it cannot overwrite an acquired offer or a match.

blocks.title: The ETA dependency on a bad day
items: At peak the matching services make about 600 batched ETA calls per second, one per request.
Each call carries about 50 candidates, so the routing engine answers about 30,000 routes per second.
Retry rounds reuse the ranked set after rechecking freshness and ownership. They do not rerun ETA in this model; three rounds do not triple the ETA fleet.
Every call carries a hard deadline of 100 ms; past it the matcher ranks the same candidates by straight-line distance and flags the match.
The degraded ratio is an alarm: a match now beats a better match in 5 seconds, but a rising ratio means the map service, not the matcher, is the incident.

blocks.text: Supply and demand per cell is computed from the same index snapshot every few seconds and published to the pricing service; matching does not call pricing, pricing reads matching's aggregates, so a pricing outage never blocks a match.
Each row names the failure, what riders and drivers see, and the mitigation.

blocks.text: At that scale the marketplace questions (batching windows, the fairness term) are product decisions with an experiment behind each, and the hard invariant is still decided in one place: one driver, one trip, and everything else in the design is allowed to degrade before that does.

blocks.caption: Billing quantities and units: conservative full-peak location volume, separate average connection occupancy.
rows: 100 binary positions of 50 bytes plus a 120-byte header make a 5-KiB frame. Flush by size or within a second; partial batches add cost excluded from this full-pack estimate.
Binary driver/session/sequence/time identifiers, coordinates, heading and flags fit the assumed fifty bytes; city/cell are derived, not repeated strings.
Custom binary packing, not KPL. Firehose transformation, JSON deaggregation and format conversion are disabled; S3 retains opaque frames for offline decoding.
Firehose bills each record rounded up to the nearest 5KB (5,120 bytes), so the 5-KiB frame is exactly one increment; KPL deaggregation would change the calculation and is not selected.
2,500 records/s each consume one 25-KiB PUT unit. On-demand ingress rounds each frame to whole KiB; both geo replicas and Firehose are three readers.
100 streams times 730 hours times $0.04 gives $2,920 before on-demand bytes.
History assumes continuous peak; WebSocket minutes assume 500,000 average connected drivers. These are deliberately different bounds.

Creation puts one index entry. Each acquisition and release changes retry_due, so each needs two index writes: delete old and put new. Final accept or cancel deletes once. Index entries stay below one KiB.

At peak the busiest city takes 174 rides a second (30 percent, assumption) and so 2,088 index writes a second, above the 1,000 write units a second one partition delivers; a global secondary index without write capacity for them would throttle the ride writes, as its page says.

The index partition key is the city plus a bucket of the ride id: 8 buckets give about 261 writes a second each at peak, and 32 give about 653 at ten times. A bucket never changes for a ride, so the writes a ride and the DynamoDB cost are unchanged; reading every bucket is a recovery query, excluded.
Creation costs two write units, each acquisition or release six, and the final accept five.
Three acquisitions and two releases make thirty units, so a ride totals thirty-seven. Failed races and recovery scans are excluded.

Ten eventual status reads, three strong driver-fence reads and three strong connection lookups. Ride version comes from the durable work item. Read items fit four KiB; write items one KiB. Recovery queries are excluded.
200 billed GB for rides, driver state and sparse pending index, derived in the next two rows. No other indexes. Connection-registry writes/storage and Lambda lifecycle costs are excluded.
One month of rides is kept (assumption): 150 million items of 1,124 bytes, a one-KiB item plus 100 bytes of per-item overhead, are about 169 GB.

Driver and session items of 1 million drivers add about 2 GB, and the pending index holds only open rides; the rest of the 200 GB is headroom for the extra overhead that transactions add (size not stated).
At an assumed three ms CPU/route, peak routing needs about ninety cores against ninety-six provisioned. No throughput guarantee; retries reuse ranking.
30 request-days and 730 instance-hours. Teaching TB is decimal; streaming bills use binary GB conversion. S3 rounds upward and uses the actual 51,200-GB breakpoint.

blocks.text: Cost per ride is the subtotal divided by the full monthly ride count, not a thousandfold larger value. The comparison is nearly linear, with WebSocket/S3 tiers and fixed NAT hours changing the curve. All task throughput and callback-byte allowances still require measurement.

L1: Location ingestion onto per-city logs with session and sequence checks, a geo index by cell, a nearest-driver query by rings.
A matching service that leases a driver, offers with a timeout, and confirms atomically; the update rate derived from the assumptions.
The one-driver-one-trip invariant decided in one place.
L2: Supply and demand per cell computed from the index and published to pricing, which never sits on the match path.
ETA as an input with a deadline and a straight-line fallback, flagged and measured.
Idempotent, fenced offers: the lease token, the compare-and-set, the rejected late accept.
Per-city partitioning of index, matching and locks, with the memory and dependency-load arithmetic.
L3: Batched assignment windows as the marketplace evolves, and the fairness term as a product decision.
Multi-cell metros with edge matching, and the tested degradation ladder when map or ETA services fail.
The fail-closed choice for the lock store, argued against availability, and the privacy retention of location history.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: what near means, the source of truth for driver state, offer timeouts, ETA, per-city partitioning, history retention. Say the numbers aloud: 250,000 location updates per second, 580 requests per second at peak, 50 candidates and one ETA batch per match, a 15 s offer round inside a 20 s confirmation target.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: DriverLocation and the cell index, DriverState with a lease token, Ride and Offer, CellStats; the location, ride and offer endpoints.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: location gateway and log, geo index per city, matching service, ETA service, lock store, rides, supply and demand to pricing. Say where the invariant is decided.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the offer protocol (compare-and-set lease, fencing token, timeouts, next candidate, three rounds), then the dependencies (ETA deadline and fallback, index freshness, pricing decoupled, the fail-closed lock store).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (batched assignment, cells of cells, degradation ladder, history and privacy), and the L3 sentence: the hard invariant is one driver, one trip, and everything else in the design is allowed to degrade before that does.
Context and scope: The cities and their driver counts, the existing location and routing services, the double-booking or slow-match incidents that motivate the design.

Goals and non-goals: Offer within 3 s, confirm within 20 s, freshness under 10 s, the invariant under every failure, degraded matching allowed; pricing computation, payments, in-trip navigation and pooling out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: the location path, the cell index, the matching flow with leases and fencing tokens, the degraded modes.

Alternatives considered: A database geo index, separate lock and ride writes reconciled later instead of one transaction, exact ETA always, broadcast offers, fail-open locks, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Privacy (location precision and retention, who may query history), security (authenticated driver identity first, then fence and offered-state validation), observability (match latency by step, degraded ratio, offer acceptance rate, index freshness per city, lock-store latency), cost (ETA calls per match as the unit cost), rollout city by city with the old matcher in shadow.
Review questions the doc must answer: What happens when a driver's accept arrives after the lease expired, and what the rider sees during a 30-second ETA service outage.
